utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please zoom in on the centre of Vukovar? A little. By one degree. Can you use crosses to mark the minefields along this part of the front line? Perhaps the usher could help you with the magic pen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: This is going to be slightly difficult, but I can make a rough sketch for you. [Marks]. This is about it. By no means everything, but most of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said yesterday there were over 50. I won't make you mark all the positions now because I know that's an impossible task. My apologies, can you hear me now? Because I think my microphone was on. Needless to say, I am not going to make you mark all the positions you mentioned yesterday; there were over 50, you said. But what I want it know is: In addition to these minefields that you have indicated, along the front lines or near the front lines, did you also -- did you also booby-trap or block any areas along the Danube?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No, not particularly. Unless you consider the area between Mitnica and Sotin to be along the banks of the Danube. It's not far from the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the Vuka? Did you lay any mines along Ivana Gorana Kovacica Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to mark those minefields near the Vuka for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move that this map be admitted into evidence. Just one question before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: These minefields, when were these laid, the ones you've just marked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: That's while I was still active on these missions, and it may have been early November or sometime around then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I move that the map be admitted into evidence before we lose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 261, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did your unit or any other unit that you heard of booby-trap the area around the Eltz Palace?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. My group didn't. If there were any mines being laid there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any minefields anywhere else in addition to what you've mentioned, the Resa restaurant at Mitnica, any minefields to prevent the enemy from crossing the Danube?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I do not know of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your group lay mines along the following check-points: Osa 1, Osa 2, and Osa 3 check-points under the command of Commander Josip Tomasevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. My group did lay mines in some of those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did your group lay mines along Patkovica Street and Kras Street and the Stjepan Supanc school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: There were no mines along Patkovica Street but there were some along Kras Street. And last but not least, there were no lines at the Stjepan Supanc school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In reply to one of the questions asked by my learned friends, you said that for the most part you would scatter mines and you explained exactly what that means. I suppose it was when you had to lay mines on top of asphalt surfaces or surfaced roads and other such areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, I think that applies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What about when you had to lay mines on the ground in areas such as gardens and cornfields? Did you not dig the mines into the ground and conceal them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No, not for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about your group in the firemen's hall sector, and did they not lay any anti-personnel mines there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about Slavonskih Brigada and Irinej? Were mines not laid between the houses so as to prevent any break-throughs by the enemy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, but only along the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if throughout October and November 1991, surprise mines, so-called surprise mines were used to booby-trap discarded weapons and tanks belonging to the JNA? Were these discarded weapons booby-trapped in any special way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No, not that I knew of. My group certainly didn't do that. I wonder if anyone at all did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You said that at one point in time you advised the members of your unit to leave town. You stayed behind with your parents. What I want to know is: Did you conceal any of the maps in your possession before you left for the hospital? Did you store them in a safe place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. I buried them in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you later find them, or did anyone else find them, and were they used when the area was cleared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The JNA soldiers found it, or the Yugoslav soldiers. After I provided them with the relevant information during one of my interviews that I was made to give while in captivity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Throughout all these activities that you've told us about, were you wearing uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: When I joined the armed forces there were no uniforms available, but I did have certain parts of the military outfit. For example, I had the boots, but there was a severe shortage of military equipment, and I did not have the full kit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You did not have the entire outfit, but did you have certain distinguishing marks or insignia that you placed on your uniform in order to display them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: We were given ZNG insignia. I didn't have time to pin them on to my clothes, to fasten them, but I did have them on me at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those who had no uniform to wear would attach these insignia to their civilian clothes, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On your group's missions was there a number of ZNG people from Nasice involved? They came to Vukovar from Nasice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were there ZNG members from any other part of Croatia, and did they have uniforms when they came to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They had better outfits than we did, those of us locals. People from the area who only got involved later on, at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This group that you belonged to, did it have permanent radio communication with the Vukovar defence headquarters, Vukovar defence command headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: You could say there was a permanent radio link. I personally had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope we're not -- we're not getting too close to revealing your identity, but I'm about to change the subject anyway. Do you know if the defence headquarters had the same sort of radio link linking them to the commands of other theatres of battle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, there was a high degree of communication by using radio links.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did units on the ground get in touch with any medical staff? For example, if somebody got wounded in the course of an operation, was there a radio link to the hospital as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember there being one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in answer to a question by my learned friend you spoke of the personnel changes in the Vukovar defence command headquarters. When Mr. Dedakovic left Vukovar, we assume that he went to Zagreb to get help. At a later time, did Mr. Dedakovic perhaps return to Vukovar with the help?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: That wasn't the only change in the command's personnel. But as far as I know, Dedakovic never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So he didn't bring any help to Vukovar, no relief, the relief that he had left in order to get?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: That's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about certain other changes to the headquarters personnel. Can you please mention any major ones and specify when they occurred, in as far as anywhere of relevance to Vukovar's defence as a whole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It's not my place to say what's relevant and what isn't, but I do know about this one replacement when Commander Soljic left and Mr. Filip Karaula replaced him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you remember the month that this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Probably sometime in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in chief yesterday about the fact that on the 16th of November you were on a mission. Were you laying mines along Kras Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Two members of your group were killed on that occasion and one was wounded. Subsequently you went straight to the Vukovar defence command headquarters, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No, it wasn't quite like that. We first evacuated the wounded and got them to the hospital, after which we evacuated the dead. The next morning I came to the headquarters, but there was no effective command anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of November, the evening of the 16th of November or the morning of the 17th, did you have a radio link to the command headquarters? Were you in touch at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: While on a mission we would often switch our radios off, or at least I did, to make sure the mission was safe. Therefore, I was not in touch with them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But at no point in time were you informed that the command -- defence command headquarters were bent on leaving town. You actually only realised once you were there and saw for yourself what the matter was; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Before the Vukovar defence command left the headquarters, do you remember if there had been a meeting held at the command at which Dr. Bosanac put forward a proposal to the effect that those who would not be joining the attempt to break out, to break through the enemy lines should go to the hospital, discard their uniforms, put on white overcoats and that she would do her best to arrange for them to join the convoy of medical staff and humanitarians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I don't know about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about once you arrived at the hospital? Did you notice that any of the wounded there were putting on white overcoats, applying plaster-casts although there was no need in order to be able to -- or, rather, in the hope of joining the medical humanitarian convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I have one more question from this set of questions before we run out of time. Yesterday you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, Your Honours, I think it might be a good idea to go into private session for this question. It relates to the witness personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. We resume tomorrow at 2.15. Hopefully in another fortnight when we have the third court available we will get a little more reasonable share of morning sittings, which may make people a lot happier. We will now adjourn for the night.
